items.concept: heart sounds; physiological splitting of S2
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 72, normal S1, normal S2 with A2 then P2 35 ms apart (a narrow split), no extra sounds, no murmur. This is the inspiratory picture of physiological splitting: S2 heard as two close components, best at the 2nd left intercostal space (pulmonic area), because P2 is soft and heard mainly at the base. At the bedside the split widens on inspiration (more venous return to the right heart delays P2, and A2 comes slightly earlier) and closes to a single S2 on expiration; the synthesiser plays the same split on every beat, so judge its width, not its movement with breathing. A split that stays audible on expiration is abnormal: wide physiological (RBBB, pulmonary stenosis, severe MR), wide fixed (ASD) or reversed (LBBB, severe AS). Next: listen with the patient sitting up through several breaths; if the split behaves abnormally, check the ECG for a bundle branch block and look for a murmur.

items.concept: wide fixed splitting of S2; atrial septal defect; pulmonary flow murmur
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 76, normal S1, a wide S2 split (A2 then P2 60 ms apart, the same on every beat) and a soft grade 2 medium-pitched blowing crescendo-decrescendo murmur confined to mid-systole. Secundum ASD: the left-to-right shunt at atrial level raises RV stroke volume, so P2 is delayed and the split is wide; it is fixed because on inspiration the extra systemic venous return is balanced by less left-to-right shunting, so RV filling and P2 timing hardly change with respiration (the synthesiser cannot vary the split with breathing; at the bedside you confirm fixedness over several breaths). The murmur is a pulmonary flow murmur at the 2nd left intercostal space, not flow through the defect; with a large shunt (Qp:Qs about 2:1 or more) a tricuspid flow mid-diastolic rumble may be heard at the left lower sternal border. Look for an RV heave and a palpable pulmonary artery; ECG: incomplete RBBB with right axis deviation (left axis suggests a primum defect). Next: transthoracic echo (RV dilatation, shunt direction, PA pressure), then transoesophageal echo or CMR to size the defect and its rims before device closure.

items.concept: paradoxical splitting of S2; left bundle branch block
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 70, soft S1, a reversed S2 split (the softer, lower-pitched P2 first, then the louder A2 50 ms later, the same on every beat), no extra sounds and no murmur. In LBBB the LV is activated late, so aortic valve closure (A2) is delayed beyond P2. On inspiration P2 moves later and fuses with A2 (single S2); on expiration the split reappears, the opposite of normal, hence 'paradoxical' (the synthesiser plays the expiratory picture on every beat). Which component comes first is inferred from this breathing behaviour, not heard directly, so the item does not ask you to tell a reversed from a wide normal-order split by ear: the clues here are a wide split of S2 (not S1) with no murmur and no click, and a soft S1. RBBB gives a split of similar width that widens further on inspiration. Heard best at the 2nd left intercostal space. Other causes of reversed splitting: RV pacing, severe aortic stenosis, obstructive HCM, acute ischaemia and a large PDA. The soft S1 fits the delayed, less forceful LV contraction (and a long PR interval, if present). Next: 12-lead ECG (QRS 120 ms or more, broad notched R waves in I, aVL, V5-V6), then echo for LV function, dyssynchrony and an aortic valve cause.

items.concept: third heart sound; ventricular gallop; heart failure
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 96, slightly soft S1, single-sounding S2, and a dull low-pitched extra sound 140 ms after S2; no murmur. That is an S3 (protodiastolic or ventricular gallop): rapid early filling suddenly checked by a dilated, volume-loaded ventricle; with the tachycardia it gives the 'Ken-tuc-ky' cadence. Listen at the apex with the bell applied lightly, patient in the left lateral position; a right-sided S3 is at the left lower sternal border and louder on inspiration. Being low pitched, it fades when the bell is pressed firmly. After about 40 years it means systolic heart failure or volume overload (also severe MR or a high-output state); in children, young adults, athletes and pregnancy it can be physiological. Do not confuse it with an opening snap (earlier, high-pitched, snapping) or a pericardial knock (earlier and higher-pitched than an S3). Next: JVP, basal crackles, oedema, displaced apex, pulsus alternans; ECG, natriuretic peptides and echo for LVEF.

items.concept: fourth heart sound; atrial gallop; LV hypertrophy
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 68, normal S1, normal-to-loud single-sounding S2, and a dull low-pitched extra sound 90 ms before S1; no murmur. That is an S4 (presystolic or atrial gallop): atrial contraction into a stiff, non-compliant left ventricle ('Ten-nes-see'). Best at the apex with the bell, patient in the left lateral position. Causes: hypertensive LVH, aortic stenosis, HCM, acute ischaemia or infarction, and ageing. It needs an atrial contraction, so it is never heard in atrial fibrillation. Distinguish it from a split S1 (both components higher-pitched, best at the left lower sternal border, not abolished by firm pressure of the bell) and from an ejection click (after S1, high-pitched, at the base). Next: blood pressure, apex beat (sustained, not displaced), fundi; ECG voltage criteria for LVH and echo for wall thickness and diastolic function.

items.concept: aortic stenosis; ejection systolic murmur; soft A2
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 66, normal S1, a very soft single S2 (A2 lost, no split; the synthesiser also softens P2, which is preserved in a patient) and a harsh medium-pitched grade 4 crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur that rises slowly, peaks late (about two thirds of the way through systole) and ends just before the soft S2; no ejection click. The synthesiser builds this late-peaking diamond from three overlapping pieces: a soft grade 2 diamond over the whole of systole, a grade 4 crescendo over mid-systole and a grade 4 decrescendo over late systole, joined without a gap at the peak. The soft first piece starts at S1; in a patient an ejection murmur starts just after S1. Severe calcific AS: maximal at the 2nd right intercostal space, radiating to both carotids (the high-frequency part may reach the apex and sound musical: Gallavardin phenomenon). Signs of severity: late peak, soft or absent A2 (single or paradoxically split S2), slow-rising small-volume pulse (parvus et tardus), sustained apex and S4; loudness is not severity (low-flow AS can be soft). The murmur gets louder with squatting, leg raise and in the beat after a pause, and softer with Valsalva and standing, the opposite of obstructive HCM. Next: carotid pulse and pulse pressure, then echo: peak velocity 4 m/s or more, mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, AVA under 1.0 cm².

items.concept: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; dynamic LVOT obstruction; Valsalva
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 70, normal S1, normal, single-sounding S2, an S4 just before S1, and a harsh medium-pitched grade 3 crescendo-decrescendo murmur confined to mid-systole (it starts well after S1 and stops before S2). Obstructive HCM: dynamic LVOT obstruction from septal hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral leaflet. Loudest at the left lower sternal border (3rd-4th left intercostal spaces), often extending to the apex, with little or no radiation to the carotids (unlike AS); an associated MR jet from SAM radiates to the axilla. The key test is dynamic (stated here, not synthesised): louder on Valsalva strain and on standing (smaller LV), softer on squatting, passive leg raise and handgrip. Associated signs: brisk jerky (spike-and-dome) carotid pulse, double or triple apical impulse, S4, and a normal A2. Next: Valsalva and squat-to-stand at the bedside, ECG (LVH, deep narrow Q waves), and echo: maximal wall thickness 15 mm or more, LVOT gradient at rest and on provocation (30 mmHg or more = obstruction).

items.title: Obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 76, soft S1, normal S2, a high-pitched blowing grade 3 plateau (holosystolic) murmur from S1 up to S2, and an S3 in early diastole. Chronic severe primary MR: the LV ejects into the low-pressure left atrium throughout systole, so the murmur is band-shaped and runs up to A2. Maximal at the apex, radiating to the left axilla; an anteriorly directed jet (posterior leaflet prolapse) can radiate to the base instead. Here the S3 marks a large regurgitant volume rather than necessarily heart failure, and a short mid-diastolic flow rumble may follow it. Louder with handgrip and transient arterial occlusion (more afterload), softer with amyl nitrite; unlike TR it does not increase on inspiration. Next: displaced, hyperdynamic apex, atrial fibrillation, signs of pulmonary hypertension; echo for the mechanism (Carpentier class), EROA (0.40 cm² or more = severe primary MR), regurgitant volume, LVEF and LV end-systolic diameter.

items.title: Chronic mitral regurgitation

items.concept: mitral valve prolapse; mid-systolic click; late systolic murmur
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 70, normal S1 and S2, a short high-pitched mid-systolic click 200 ms after S1, then a high-pitched blowing grade 2 late systolic crescendo murmur running up to S2. Mitral valve prolapse: the click is the sudden tensing of the redundant leaflet and chordae as the leaflet billows into the left atrium; the murmur is the MR that follows. Best at the apex, listened to supine and standing. Dynamic test: on standing or Valsalva (smaller LV) the click moves towards S1 and the murmur lengthens; on squatting the click moves later and the murmur shortens. MVP and obstructive HCM are the two lesions that grow with less preload; the click and the apical site separate them. Look for a thin habitus, pectus excavatum, straight back and Marfan features. Next: echo (leaflet displacement of 2 mm or more beyond the annular plane in the parasternal long axis, leaflet thickness, MR severity, annular disjunction) and ask about palpitations and syncope (ventricular arrhythmias).

items.title: Mitral valve prolapse: mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur

items.concept: mitral stenosis; opening snap; mid-diastolic rumble
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 72 (sinus rhythm), loud S1, normal S2, a sharp high-pitched opening snap 80 ms after A2, then, starting right after the snap, a low-pitched rumbling grade 3 mid-diastolic decrescendo murmur followed by a grade 3 low-pitched rumbling late diastolic crescendo (presystolic accentuation) running into S1. Rheumatic MS in sinus rhythm: the gradient across the narrowed valve persists through diastole and rises again with atrial contraction (the presystolic accentuation is lost in atrial fibrillation). The rumble is localised at the apex: bell applied lightly, left lateral position, after a little exercise; it does not radiate. The opening snap is best between the apex and the left lower sternal border. The shorter the A2-OS interval (80 ms here, midway in the usual 40-120 ms range; under about 70-80 ms suggests severe MS, over about 100-120 ms mild MS) and the longer the rumble, the tighter the stenosis. The shape asked about is that of the mid-diastolic rumble: decrescendo, with presystolic accentuation. The synthesiser lets the rumble fade out briefly in mid-diastole before the presystolic crescendo; a rumble that persists right up to S1 means a tighter stenosis. Next: rhythm (AF), loud P2, RV heave, Graham Steell murmur (pulmonary hypertension); echo: MVA by planimetry or pressure half-time (1.5 cm² or less = clinically significant), mean gradient, PA pressure and valve anatomy (Wilkins score) for balloon commissurotomy.

items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 70, slightly soft S1, normal S2, and a high-pitched blowing grade 3 decrescendo murmur that starts immediately with A2 and fades over the first third of diastole. Chronic AR: the aortic-to-LV diastolic gradient is highest at the start of diastole and then falls, hence the decrescendo. Best at the left sternal edge, 3rd-4th intercostal space, with the diaphragm, patient sitting up and leaning forward with the breath held in expiration; loudest at the right sternal edge suggests aortic root disease (dilatation, dissection) rather than a valve lesion. Louder with handgrip and squatting, softer with amyl nitrite. A longer murmur means more severe chronic AR (in acute AR it is short and soft). Look for a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse, wide pulse pressure, displaced apex, de Musset, Quincke and Duroziez signs, a systolic flow murmur (to-and-fro) and an apical Austin Flint rumble. Next: blood pressure and peripheral signs, then echo: vena contracta over 6 mm, holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta, LV size (LVESD over 50 mm) and LVEF.

items.concept: Austin Flint murmur; aortic regurgitation; mid-diastolic rumble
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 70, soft S1, normal S2, no opening snap; a low-pitched rumbling grade 3 mid-diastolic decrescendo murmur (the same shape as the MS rumble), plus a softer high-pitched blowing grade 2 early diastolic decrescendo murmur starting at A2. The questions refer to the louder apical rumble; the early diastolic murmur is the clue to its cause. Austin Flint murmur of severe AR: the regurgitant jet strikes the anterior mitral leaflet and the rapidly rising LV diastolic pressure narrows the mitral inflow, producing a functional mid-diastolic (sometimes presystolic) rumble at the apex. It mimics MS, and its shape does not separate the two: S1 is soft and there is no opening snap, and it gets softer with amyl nitrite (less AR) whereas the rumble of MS gets louder. Its presence marks the AR as severe; in a patient the AR murmur of severe AR is long, often holodiastolic (the synthesiser plays it over the first third of diastole only). Next: collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure and the other peripheral AR signs; echo shows a normal, non-stenotic mitral valve with severe AR (and possibly fluttering of the anterior mitral leaflet).

items.concept: ventricular septal defect; holosystolic murmur; thrill
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 84, normal S1, normal, single-sounding S2, and a loud harsh high-pitched grade 4 plateau (holosystolic) murmur from S1 to S2; no extra sounds. Restrictive (small) perimembranous or muscular VSD: a high LV-to-RV pressure gradient throughout systole. Maximal at the left lower sternal border (about the 4th left intercostal space), localised to the left sternal border (a loud one may be heard more widely), without axillary radiation, with a palpable thrill (grade 4). Loudness is inversely related to defect size: a small defect can be grade 4-5 (maladie de Roger). Louder with handgrip, softer with amyl nitrite, and no increase on inspiration (unlike TR). In a large VSD with rising pulmonary pressure the murmur shortens and softens and P2 becomes loud; in Eisenmenger physiology there is no shunt murmur, with cyanosis and a loud single S2. Next: thrill, signs of LV volume load (displaced apex, apical mid-diastolic flow rumble when Qp:Qs is about 2:1 or more), an AR murmur (aortic cusp prolapse in outlet or perimembranous defects); echo for site, size, gradient and PA pressure.

extra.label: Wide split S2 (A2 then P2; wide or fixed)

location.label: Left infraclavicular area (below the left clavicle)

items.concept: patent ductus arteriosus; continuous machinery murmur
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 84, normal S1 and S2, and a harsh medium-pitched grade 3 continuous crescendo-decrescendo murmur that rises through systole, peaks at S2 (which it partly hides) and fades through diastole: the 'machinery' (Gibson) murmur. PDA: aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary arterial pressure in both systole and diastole, so flow and murmur are continuous. Best in the left infraclavicular area (1st-2nd left intercostal space), radiating to the back. A large shunt adds a collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure, displaced apex and an apical flow rumble; as pulmonary vascular resistance rises the diastolic part shortens and disappears (and differential cyanosis appears in Eisenmenger physiology). Other continuous murmurs: venous hum (neck, abolished by jugular compression or lying flat), coronary AV fistula (lower on the chest, often diastolic accentuation), ruptured sinus of Valsalva (sudden onset); combined AS and AR is to-and-fro with a gap at S2, not continuous. Next: pulses and pulse pressure, then echo (ductal flow into the pulmonary artery, LA and LV size, PA pressure).

items.concept: pulmonary stenosis; pulmonary ejection click; wide split S2
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 72, normal S1, a sharp high-pitched ejection click 60 ms after S1, a harsh medium-pitched grade 3 crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur that starts with the click, peaks in mid-to-late systole and runs through A2 up to the delayed P2, and a wide S2 split (A2, then a softer P2 50 ms later). Valvular (doming) pulmonary stenosis: the click is the stenotic valve snapping open to its limit; the murmur is maximal at the 2nd left intercostal space (pulmonic area), radiating toward the left shoulder and the left side of the neck, and P2 is delayed by the prolonged RV ejection; a murmur that runs through A2 to P2 separates moderate PS from AS, whose murmur ends at A2. The pulmonary ejection click is the only right-sided event that gets softer on inspiration (the higher RV end-diastolic pressure partly opens the valve before systole), while the murmur itself gets louder. Severity: the later the murmur peaks and the closer the click to S1, the tighter the stenosis; in severe PS P2 becomes soft and late, the click may disappear, and an RV heave and a giant a wave appear. Next: JVP a wave, RV heave, Noonan features; ECG (RVH) and echo: peak velocity over 4 m/s (peak gradient over 64 mmHg) = severe.

items.concept: innocent murmur; flow murmur; features of an innocent murmur
items.explanation: Synthesised: HR 84, normal S1, normal, single-sounding S2 (not wide), and a soft grade 2 medium-pitched blowing crescendo-decrescendo murmur confined to mid-systole; no click and no extra sounds. An innocent (physiological flow) murmur: brisk ejection across a normal pulmonary (or aortic) valve, common in children, adolescents, pregnancy, fever, anaemia and thyrotoxicosis. Heard at the 2nd-3rd left intercostal space, localised, loudest supine and softer on sitting or standing. What makes it innocent: systolic, grade 1-2, short, normal S1 and S2 with normal splitting, no click, no thrill, normal pulses and apex, and no symptoms. Compare ASD (the same flow murmur with a wide fixed split) and pulmonary stenosis (ejection click, harsher and longer murmur). Any diastolic murmur, a grade 3 or louder murmur, a thrill, an abnormal S2, a click or symptoms: get an echo.
